answer:
**Hard voting discards confidence before combining models; soft voting combines confidence first.** Suppose three binary models predict positive probabilities 0.51, 0.51, and 0.01. Hard voting chooses positive because two models cross 0.5. Soft voting averages to about 0.343 and chooses negative. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html)

Neither result is automatically correct. The third model might have decisive evidence, or it might be badly overconfident. Soft voting benefits from comparable, useful probabilities; hard voting can be less vulnerable to extreme scales but throws away meaningful differences in confidence.

Weighted variants give different influence to each model. Estimate weights and calibration using held-out or out-of-fold predictions, not the final test labels. Align class ordering before averaging so one model's class-zero column is not mistaken for another's class-one column.

Diversity matters: models making the same errors add little independent information. For cost-sensitive decisions or abstention, validate a threshold on the aggregate score rather than assuming 0.5 is universally appropriate.

**Technical details and references.**

Hard voting takes each model's predicted class and chooses the majority or weighted majority. Soft voting averages class probabilities and chooses the largest aggregate probability, retaining confidence information. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html)

Soft voting can improve decisions when probabilities are reasonably comparable, but an overconfident miscalibrated model can dominate. Weighting and calibration must be learned on held-out/out-of-fold predictions, not the final test set. Align class order and handle missing classes consistently. Diversity matters: averaging many identical errors gives little benefit. For abstention or cost-sensitive decisions, use the aggregated probabilities with an explicitly validated threshold rule.
